# How to use this guide

Pharma Marketing Management is **one of the semester-8 electives** of the PCI B.Pharm course. It has no practical; the whole subject is the 75-mark theory paper. The subject is descriptive: there are very few calculations, and marks come from well-organised answers with definitions, classifications, diagrams and pharmaceutical examples. Study one unit a day: read the notes, draw each diagram once from memory (marketing environment, BCG matrix, product life cycle, channel chain), then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus papers.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 4 joins two syllabus topics (marketing channels and the professional sales representative) and Unit 5 joins pricing with emerging concepts, as the syllabus itself does.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a diagram or table and pharmaceutical examples.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Marketing and the pharma market | Marketing vs selling, marketing environment, consumer and industrial buying behaviour, segmentation and targeting, prescribing habits of doctors, market research |
| 2 Product decisions | Product life cycle, product mix and line decisions, BCG matrix, positioning, new product development, branding, packaging and labelling, product manager |
| 3 Promotion | Promotional mix and its determinants, promotional budget methods, sampling, medical exhibitions, public relations, online promotion of OTC products |
| 4 Channels and PSR | Channel design and members, channel conflict, physical distribution tasks, duties of PSR, detailing, selection, training, evaluation and compensation |
| 5 Pricing and emerging concepts | Pricing objectives, determinants, methods and strategies, DPCO and NPPA, vertical and horizontal marketing, rural marketing, consumerism, global marketing |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Open every answer with a one-line definition, then a classification table or list. Examiners in marketing papers reward structure.
2. Draw where you can: the marketing environment circles, Porter's five forces, the product life cycle curve, the BCG grid, the channel chain from manufacturer to patient, the buyer decision process. A neat diagram is worth marks even in a short answer.
3. Always bring the answer back to medicines: name the doctor, chemist, stockist, C&F agent, OTC versus prescription products. A general business-studies answer scores less than one with pharmacy examples.
4. For comparison questions (marketing vs selling, push vs pull, skimming vs penetration, vertical vs horizontal systems), use a two-column table with at least six points.
5. Learn the few exact facts that this paper can test: DPCO is issued under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955; current order DPCO 2013; ceiling price = simple average PTR of brands with at least 1% market share plus 16% retailer margin; annual WPI revision; 10% annual limit on MRP increase for non-scheduled drugs; NPPA set up on 29 August 1997.
6. Do not write market-size or growth figures unless you remember them with their source and year; a wrong number costs more than no number.
7. In long PSR questions, cover all the syllabus words in order — duties, purpose of detailing, selection and training, supervising, call norms, motivating, evaluating, compensation, future prospects — with two or three points each.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five answers with a diagram or table each: **marketing environment (micro and macro)**, **product life cycle with strategies at each stage**, **promotional mix and its determinants**, **duties, selection, training and compensation of the PSR**, and **DPCO and NPPA**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Definitions in one line**

| Term | One-line meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Marketing | Identifying customer needs and satisfying them profitably through product, price, place and promotion |
| Market | All actual and potential buyers of a product |
| Segmentation | Dividing a market into groups of buyers with similar needs |
| Targeting | Choosing which segments to serve |
| Positioning | Giving a product a clear, distinctive place in the customer's mind |
| Product mix | All product lines and items a company sells (width, length, depth, consistency) |
| Brand | Name, sign or symbol that identifies a seller's product |
| Promotion | Seller's communication to inform, persuade and remind |
| Detailing | Planned scientific presentation of a product to a doctor |
| Marketing channel | Set of organisations that make a product available to the user |
| Physical distribution | Planning and controlling the flow of goods to the point of use |
| Ceiling price | Maximum price notified by the government for a scheduled formulation |
| Consumerism | Movement to protect and strengthen buyers' rights |

**Lists to write without thinking**

| Topic | Items |
| --- | --- |
| Marketing concepts | Production, product, selling, marketing, societal marketing |
| Micro-environment | Company, suppliers, intermediaries, customers, competitors, publics |
| Macro-environment | Demographic, economic, political–legal, technological, social–cultural, natural |
| Porter's forces | Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power |
| Buyer decision | Need recognition → information search → evaluation → purchase → post-purchase |
| Segmentation bases | Geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioural, prescriber-based |
| PLC stages | Introduction, growth, maturity, decline |
| BCG matrix | Star, cash cow, question mark, dog |
| New product process | Idea → screening → concept test → strategy → business analysis → development → test marketing → commercialisation |
| Packaging functions | Protect, identify, inform, convenience, safety, promote, aid compliance |
| Promotional mix | Personal selling, advertising, sales promotion, PR, direct marketing, digital |
| Budget methods | Affordable, % of sales, competitive parity, objective-and-task |
| Channel chain (India) | Manufacturer → C&F agent → stockist → retailer → patient |
| Distribution intensity | Intensive, selective, exclusive |
| Channel conflict | Vertical, horizontal, multichannel |
| PD tasks | Order processing, warehousing, inventory, transport, handling, returns |
| PSR syllabus words | Duties, detailing, selection, training, supervising, call norms, motivation, evaluation, compensation, prospects |
| Pricing objectives | Survival, profit, ROI, share, quality leadership, meeting competition, social |
| Pricing methods | Cost-plus, break-even, perceived value, going rate, sealed bid |
| VMS types | Corporate, contractual, administered |
| Consumer rights | Safety, information, choice, to be heard, redressal, education |
| Global entry modes | Export, licensing, joint venture, direct investment |

**Facts examiners can check**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| DPCO issued under | Section 3, Essential Commodities Act, 1955 |
| Earlier DPCOs | 1970, 1979, 1987, 1995 (cost-based) |
| Current order | DPCO 2013, based on National Pharmaceutical Pricing Policy 2012 |
| Scheduled formulations | Medicines in the National List of Essential Medicines (First Schedule) |
| Ceiling price formula | Simple average PTR of brands with ≥1% market share + 16% retailer margin |
| Annual revision | 1 April, by wholesale price index |
| Non-scheduled drugs | MRP rise limited to 10% a year |
| NPPA set up | 29 August 1997, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers |
| Advertising law | Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954; Schedule J of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules |
| Marketing code | Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (2014, revised 2024) |
| Consumer law | Consumer Protection Act, 2019 |
| Break-even units | Fixed cost ÷ (price − variable cost per unit) |

**One-line contrasts examiners like**

| Pair | Difference |
| --- | --- |
| Marketing vs selling | Starts from customer needs vs starts from the product in the factory |
| Consumer vs industrial buying | Individual, small, emotional vs group (buying centre), large, technical, tender-based |
| Push vs pull | Promotion aimed at channel and prescribers vs aimed at final consumers |
| Skimming vs penetration | High launch price vs low launch price |
| Product line vs product mix | Related group of products vs all products of the company |
| Primary vs secondary pack | In contact with the product vs carton around it |
| C&F agent vs stockist | Works on commission, does not own goods vs buys, owns and resells stock |
| Vertical vs horizontal marketing | Different levels act as one system vs same-level firms combine |
| DPCO vs NPPA | The legal pricing order vs the authority that enforces it |
| Salary vs commission plan | Security and control vs incentive with insecurity |

**Diagrams to practise once tonight**

1. Marketing environment: company inside micro inside macro.
2. Porter's five forces.
3. Product life cycle curve with sales and profit lines.
4. BCG matrix with the four boxes.
5. Channel chain from manufacturer to patient.
6. Buyer decision process arrow chain.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: marketing is identifying customer needs and satisfying them profitably through product, price, place and promotion.
2. Marketing environment: all forces outside marketing management that affect its ability to build relations with target customers.
3. Diagram: company (internal) inside the micro-environment, inside the macro-environment.
4. Micro-environment: company departments (R&D, production, quality, finance); suppliers of APIs, excipients and packing material; intermediaries (C&F agents, stockists, chemists, transporters, advertising agencies); customers (doctors, patients, hospitals, government); competitors; publics (media, government, community, investors).
5. Macro-environment: demographic (ageing, lifestyle diseases, urbanisation); economic (income, out-of-pocket spending, insurance); political–legal (Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, DPCO, patent and advertising laws, marketing code); technological (new delivery systems, biologics, e-pharmacy, digital detailing); social–cultural (health awareness, self-medication, traditional medicine); natural (waste rules, disease patterns).
6. Micro forces can be partly influenced; macro forces cannot be controlled, only adapted to.
7. SWOT analysis links the environment with the company: internal strengths and weaknesses, external opportunities and threats.
8. Importance: spotting opportunities, avoiding threats, planning the marketing mix, regulatory compliance.
questions.question: Define marketing. Explain the marketing environment of a pharmaceutical company with a suitable diagram.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: dividing a market into distinct groups of buyers with similar needs or characteristics who may need separate products or marketing mixes.
2. Need: no single offer suits all doctors and patients; resources can be focused.
3. Bases: geographic (region, urban/rural, climate — rural division with low-cost packs); demographic (age, sex, income — paediatric syrups, products for women, geriatric products); psychographic (lifestyle, values — health-conscious buyers of supplements); behavioural (usage rate, loyalty, benefit sought — chronic vs acute users); prescriber-based (speciality, prescribing volume — cardiologists, gynaecologists, GPs).
4. Requirements of a useful segment: measurable, substantial, accessible, differentiable, actionable.
5. Targeting: evaluate segment size, growth, competition and fit with company resources; select segments.
6. Strategies: undifferentiated (one offer for all); differentiated (separate divisions per speciality); concentrated or niche (only oncology); micromarketing (local or individual).
7. Then positioning: STP = segmentation → targeting → positioning.
8. Benefits: better use of field force, focused promotion, higher customer satisfaction, identification of gaps.
questions.question: What is market segmentation? Discuss the bases of segmentation and targeting strategies with examples from the pharmaceutical market.

questions.answer:
1. Consumer buying behaviour: how individuals buy for personal use; in pharma mainly OTC products and choice of doctor and chemist.
2. Factors: cultural (culture, subculture, class), social (family, reference groups, roles), personal (age, occupation, income, lifestyle), psychological (motivation, perception, learning, beliefs).
3. Decision process: need recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase → post-purchase behaviour (example of buying an antacid).
4. Industrial buying behaviour: purchases by organisations such as hospitals, government stores and companies buying APIs.
5. Features: fewer, larger buyers; derived demand; technical specifications; tenders and contracts; long-term relationships.
6. Buying centre: users, influencers (pharmacy and therapeutics committee), buyers, deciders, gatekeepers.
7. Buying situations: straight rebuy, modified rebuy, new task; stages from problem recognition to performance review.
8. Differences (table): individual vs group decision; small vs large quantities; emotional vs rational and technical; informal vs formal procedure; advertising vs personal selling and tenders.
questions.question: Discuss consumer buying behaviour and industrial buying behaviour. How do they differ in the pharmaceutical context?

questions.answer:
1. Starting point: selling starts from the factory and existing product; marketing starts from the market and customer needs.
2. Focus: seller's need to convert product into cash vs buyer's needs and satisfaction.
3. Time view: short-term volume vs long-term relationship and loyalty.
4. Means: selling and promotion push vs integrated marketing mix (4 Ps).
5. End: profit through sales volume vs profit through customer satisfaction.
6. Scope: selling is one part of marketing; marketing is wider.
7. One-liner: selling makes customers want what the company has; marketing makes what customers want.
questions.question: Differentiate between marketing and selling.

questions.answer:
1. Efficacy and safety of the drug from evidence and personal experience.
2. Company image for quality and consistency.
3. Information sources: medical representatives, journals, CME and conferences, colleagues, key opinion leaders.
4. Patient factors: affordability, dosing convenience, palatability for children.
5. Availability of the brand at nearby chemists.
6. Habit and brand loyalty.
7. Service: regular, informed visits and scientific literature.
8. Motivation: better outcomes, reputation, updated knowledge; gifts and inducements are restricted by ethics rules.
questions.question: Explain the factors that influence the prescribing habits of physicians.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: systematic design, collection, analysis and reporting of data for a marketing decision.
2. Process: define problem → plan research → collect data → analyse → report.
3. Secondary data (sales records, retail and prescription audits, reports) and primary data (surveys of doctors and chemists, interviews, focus groups, test marketing).
4. Uses: estimating demand for a new product; studying prescribing behaviour and brand share; testing brand names, packs and messages; measuring promotional effect; studying competitors and prices; finding unmet needs; sales forecasting and territory planning.
questions.question: Describe the role of market research in the pharmaceutical industry.

questions.answer:
1. Rivalry among existing firms: intense because many companies sell branded generics of the same molecule.
2. Threat of new entrants: barriers are GMP investment, licences, field force, doctors' brand loyalty.
3. Threat of substitutes: other molecules of the class, traditional medicines, non-drug therapy.
4. Bargaining power of buyers: high for hospitals, tenders and chains; low for individual patients.
5. Bargaining power of suppliers: high when APIs come from few sources.
6. Diagram: rivalry at the centre with the four forces around it.
7. Use: judging the attractiveness of a therapy segment.
questions.question: Explain Porter's five forces model of industry analysis with reference to the pharmaceutical industry.

questions.answer:
1. Physician: reputation and recommendation by family and friends; qualification and speciality; distance and availability; fees; behaviour and time given; hospital attachment.
2. Pharmacist: nearness to home or clinic; availability of all prescribed items; price and discounts; trust and advice; home delivery; opening hours; credit for regular customers.
3. The pharmacist influences OTC purchases and generic choice, so retail relations matter to marketers.
questions.question: What factors influence a patient's choice of physician and retail pharmacist?

questions.answer: The set of controllable tools a company combines to get the desired response from its target market: product, price, place and promotion (the 4 Ps).
questions.question: Define the marketing mix.

questions.answer: Satisfying customer needs profitably while also protecting the long-term welfare of society; it suits medicines because public health and rational use matter.
questions.question: What is the societal marketing concept?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: the course of a product's sales and profits over its life in the market.
2. Diagram: S-shaped sales curve through introduction, growth, maturity and decline, with a profit curve starting below zero.
3. Introduction: low sales, losses due to launch cost, few competitors; create awareness through detailing, samples, launch meetings and CME.
4. Growth: rapid sales rise, rising profit, competitors enter; build brand preference, widen distribution, add strengths.
5. Maturity: peak and levelling sales, highest profit, many branded generics; defend share with reminder promotion, line extensions, new indications, pack changes, trade schemes.
6. Decline: falling sales and profit; cut costs, harvest, or withdraw; shift to low-cost or rural segments.
7. Extending the life cycle: new indication, new dosage form or delivery system, rational combinations, new packs, new markets, Rx-to-OTC switch where permitted.
8. Pharma feature: patent expiry causes a sharp fall for the innovator; many brands of one molecule are in maturity at once.
questions.question: Explain the product life cycle with a diagram. Discuss the marketing strategies used at each stage for a pharmaceutical product.

questions.answer:
1. Brand: name, sign, symbol or design identifying a seller's product; trademark is its legally protected form.
2. Benefits of branding: identification, loyalty and repeat prescription, premium, legal protection, easier launches.
3. Good brand name: short, easy to say and remember, distinctive, not confused with other drug names (avoids dispensing errors), suggests benefit without false claims, registrable, acceptable across languages.
4. Branding strategies: individual names, family brand, company + individual name, brand extension, unbranded generic, co-marketing; brand equity.
5. Packaging levels: primary (blister, bottle, ampoule), secondary (carton), tertiary (shipping box).
6. Functions: protection from light, moisture, oxygen and breakage; identification; convenience; tamper-evident and child-resistant safety; promotion; compliance.
7. Packaging decisions: material, form, pack size, design and colour, cost, stability compatibility, environment.
8. Labelling: must follow the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945; carries product names, content, net quantity, batch number, licence number, manufacturing and expiry dates, manufacturer's name and address, MRP and schedule warnings.
9. Marketing role of labels: identify, grade, describe, promote, give legal directions and warnings.
questions.question: Discuss branding, packaging and labelling decisions for pharmaceutical products.

questions.answer:
1. New product: new-to-the-world product, new line, addition to a line, improvement, repositioned product or lower-cost version.
2. Sources in pharma: in-house R&D, in-licensing, acquisition, co-marketing, new formulations and combinations, generics after patent expiry.
3. Stages: idea generation → idea screening → concept development and testing → marketing strategy → business analysis → product development (formulation, stability, approval) → test marketing → commercialisation.
4. Adoption by doctors: awareness, interest, evaluation, trial, adoption; adopter groups innovators to laggards.
5. Reasons for failure: overestimated market, poor positioning, no real advantage, wrong timing, high price, weak promotion, regulatory delay, quality problems.
6. Ways to reduce failure: market research, careful screening, clear USP, proper launch planning.
questions.question: What is a new product? Describe the stages of new product development and the reasons why new products fail.

questions.answer:
1. Portfolio tool plotting relative market share (horizontal) against market growth rate (vertical).
2. Star: high growth, high share; invest to grow.
3. Cash cow: low growth, high share; generates cash for other products.
4. Question mark: high growth, low share; invest selectively or drop.
5. Dog: low growth, low share; harvest or divest.
6. Diagram: 2 × 2 grid.
7. Use: deciding which brands to fund, hold or prune; limitation: uses only two factors.
questions.question: Explain the BCG growth–share matrix with a diagram.

questions.answer:
1. Product line: group of closely related products (all anti-diabetic brands of a company).
2. Product mix: all lines and items a company sells; dimensions width, length, depth, consistency.
3. Line decisions: line length; line stretching (downward, upward, two-way); line filling (new strength, paediatric form); line modernisation; line featuring; line pruning of weak items.
4. Mix strategies: expansion, contraction, alteration, line extension.
questions.question: Define product line and product mix. Explain product line decisions.

questions.answer:
1. Positioning: giving a product a clear, distinctive and desirable place in the target customer's mind relative to competitors.
2. Bases: attribute (once-daily, sugar-free), benefit (faster relief, better compliance), use, user (elderly, pregnancy), against a competitor, quality/price, product class.
3. Steps: identify advantages, select the right ones, communicate consistently.
4. Perceptual map and USP.
5. Claims must be backed by evidence and approved information.
questions.question: What is product positioning? Describe the bases of positioning a pharmaceutical brand.

questions.answer:
1. Product manager is responsible for a group of brands like a mini general manager.
2. Studies market, competitors and prescription trends.
3. Prepares the annual brand plan: objectives, target doctors, positioning, budget, forecast.
4. Designs promotional inputs: visual aids, literature, samples, digital material.
5. Trains medical representatives on product knowledge.
6. Coordinates sales, production, medical, regulatory, finance and distribution.
7. Plans launches and line extensions; monitors sales and market share; handles field feedback.
8. Weakness: responsibility without full authority over the field force.
questions.question: Describe the role and duties of a product manager in a pharmaceutical company.

questions.answer:
1. Legal status: prescription (scheduled — H, H1, X) and OTC products.
2. Patent status: patented, branded generics, unbranded generics.
3. Therapeutic class: anti-infectives, cardiac, anti-diabetic, analgesics, respiratory, gastrointestinal, vitamins.
4. Dosage form: tablets, capsules, liquids, injections, topicals, inhalers.
5. Nature: small molecules, biologics and biosimilars, vaccines.
6. Buyer: retail vs institutional.
7. Therapy duration: acute vs chronic.
8. Importance: decides promotional route, channel and pricing.
questions.question: Classify pharmaceutical products for marketing purposes.

questions.answer: Core benefit (relief or cure), actual product (brand, dosage form, pack, quality) and augmented product (information, service, support programmes).
questions.question: What are the three levels of a product?

questions.answer: Using an existing successful brand name for a new form, strength or combination, such as launching a sustained-release or paediatric version of an established brand.
questions.question: What is a line extension? Give an example.

questions.answer:
1. Promotion: seller's communication to inform, persuade and remind; AIDA model.
2. Promotional mix tools: personal selling (detailing by MRs — main tool for prescription drugs); advertising (journals to professionals, mass media only for OTC); sales promotion (samples, trade schemes, OTC offers); public relations (camps, awareness, press); direct marketing (direct mail, e-mail); digital (websites, social media, e-detailing).
3. Determinants: type of product (Rx vs OTC); type of target (few technical buyers vs mass consumers); product life cycle stage; buyer readiness stage; push or pull strategy; budget; competition; legal and ethical rules.
4. Push vs pull: Rx drugs pushed through doctors and channel; OTC pulled by consumer demand.
5. Integrated marketing communication: all tools give one consistent message.
6. Ethics: accurate, balanced, evidence-based claims; no inducements; UCPMP.

2. History: DPCOs of 1970, 1979, 1987 and 1995 were cost-based (cost of manufacture plus allowance); DPCO 2013 is based on the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Policy, 2012.
3. Scope: medicines in the National List of Essential Medicines form the First Schedule (scheduled formulations).
4. Ceiling price: simple average of PTR of all brands and generics with market share of 1% or more, plus 16% notional retailer margin; notified in the Gazette.
5. Annual revision on 1 April by the wholesale price index.
6. Non-scheduled drugs: MRP increase limited to 10% a year.
7. New drugs: retail price fixed by the government; special powers in public interest; limited-period exemption for certain patented new drugs from Indian research; overcharged amounts recovered with interest.
8. NPPA: set up by government resolution on 29 August 1997; attached to the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers.

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Marketing and the pharmaceutical market

A medicine can be well made and still fail if nobody knows about it, the wrong people are told about it, or it does not reach the shop. Marketing is the set of activities that connects a company's products with the people who need them. In the pharmaceutical industry this is unusual, because the person who decides (the doctor), the person who pays (the patient, an insurer or the government) and the person who consumes (the patient) are often different. This unit covers the basic ideas of marketing and then looks at the pharmaceutical market and its customers.

## 1.1 Definition and general concepts of marketing

**Marketing** is the process of finding out what customers need and want, developing products that satisfy those needs, and delivering them at a price and place that suits the customer, while earning a profit for the organisation.

- The American Marketing Association describes marketing as the activity and processes for creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners and society.
- Philip Kotler describes it as a social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating and exchanging products and value with others.

**Core concepts**

| Concept | Meaning | Pharmacy example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Need | A basic state of felt deprivation | Relief from pain or fever |
| Want | The form a need takes, shaped by culture and person | A particular paracetamol brand |
| Demand | A want backed by ability and willingness to pay | Patients who can buy the prescribed brand |
| Product / offering | Anything offered to satisfy a need | Tablet, syrup, diagnostic kit, service |
| Value | Benefits received compared with cost | Effective, well-tolerated, affordable drug |
| Exchange | Getting something by offering something in return | Medicine for money at the chemist |
| Market | All actual and potential buyers of a product | All diabetic patients and their doctors |

**The marketing mix (4 Ps)** — the controllable tools a company uses:

| P | Decisions | Unit in this subject |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product | Range, quality, brand, pack, label | Unit 2 |
| Price | List price, margins, discounts, regulation | Unit 5 |
| Place | Channels, stockists, physical distribution | Unit 4 |
| Promotion | Detailing, sampling, journals, exhibitions, PR | Unit 3 |

For services, three more Ps are often added: **people, process and physical evidence**.

**Marketing management philosophies (orientations)**

1. **Production concept** — customers prefer products that are widely available and cheap; focus on efficient production.
2. **Product concept** — customers prefer the best quality; focus on improving the product, risk of "marketing myopia" (loving the product, forgetting the need).
3. **Selling concept** — customers will not buy enough unless pushed; focus on aggressive selling.
4. **Marketing concept** — find the needs of target customers and satisfy them better than competitors.
5. **Societal marketing concept** — satisfy customers while also protecting the long-term welfare of society. This is the most suitable for medicines, since public health, rational drug use and ethics matter.

## 1.2 Scope of marketing

Marketing covers much more than selling:

- Market research and forecasting of demand
- Product planning and development of new products
- Branding, packaging and labelling
- Pricing decisions within legal limits
- Selecting channels and managing distribution
- Promotion: personal selling, advertising, sampling, public relations
- Sales management: recruiting, training and controlling the field force
- After-sales service and customer relations (product complaints, pharmacovigilance reports passed to the right department)
- Marketing control: comparing results with targets

In a pharmaceutical company the marketing department usually has **product management** (product managers and brand managers), **sales** (field force), **market research**, **medical services** and **distribution/logistics** working together.

## 1.3 Marketing versus selling

| Point | Selling | Marketing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting point | Factory, existing product | Market, customer needs |
| Focus | Seller's need to convert product to cash | Buyer's needs and satisfaction |
| Time view | Short term, volume today | Long term, relationship and loyalty |
| Means | Selling and promotion push | Integrated marketing mix |
| End | Profit through sales volume | Profit through customer satisfaction |
| Scope | Narrow — one part of marketing | Wide — includes selling |

**Remember the one-liner:** selling tries to get customers to want what the company has; marketing tries to make what customers want.

## 1.4 Marketing environment

The marketing environment is all the forces outside marketing management that affect its ability to build and keep good relations with target customers.

```text
            MACRO-ENVIRONMENT (cannot control)
   Demographic  Economic  Political-legal  Technological
   Social-cultural  Natural/ecological
        +--------------------------------------+
        |       MICRO-ENVIRONMENT               |
        |  Suppliers   Intermediaries           |
        |  Competitors  Customers  Publics      |
        |     +--------------------------+      |
        |     |  COMPANY (internal):     |      |
        |     |  marketing mix, R&D,     |      |
        |     |  production, finance     |      |
        |     +--------------------------+      |
        +--------------------------------------+
```

**Micro-environment (close to the company)**

- **Company itself** — top management, R&D, production, quality, finance.
- **Suppliers** — of active ingredients (APIs), excipients, packing material.
- **Marketing intermediaries** — C&F (carrying and forwarding) agents, stockists (wholesalers), retail chemists, hospital pharmacies, transporters, advertising agencies.
- **Customers** — doctors, patients, hospitals, institutions, government tenders.
- **Competitors** — companies with similar molecules or therapeutic alternatives.
- **Publics** — media, government, financial bodies, local community, citizen groups.

**Macro-environment (wider society)**

| Force | Pharmaceutical examples |
| --- | --- |
| Demographic | Growing elderly population, rising lifestyle diseases, urbanisation |
| Economic | Income levels, out-of-pocket spending, health insurance coverage |
| Political–legal | Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules, price control (DPCO), patent law, advertising law, ethics codes |
| Technological | New delivery systems, biologics, e-pharmacy, digital detailing |
| Social–cultural | Health awareness, self-medication, preference for traditional systems |
| Natural | Environmental rules on manufacturing waste, climate-related disease patterns |

**SWOT analysis** links the environment to the company: internal **strengths and weaknesses**, external **opportunities and threats**.

## 1.5 Industry and competitive analysis

**Porter's five forces** explain how attractive (profitable) an industry is:

```text
                 Threat of new entrants
                          |
  Bargaining power  -> RIVALRY AMONG  <- Bargaining power
  of suppliers         EXISTING FIRMS      of buyers
                          |
                 Threat of substitutes
```

| Force | In pharma |
| --- | --- |
| Rivalry | Many companies sell branded generics of the same molecule, so rivalry is intense |
| New entrants | Barriers: GMP investment, licences, field force, brand loyalty of doctors; lower for third-party (contract) manufacturing |
| Substitutes | Other molecules in the same class, traditional medicines, non-drug therapy |
| Buyer power | Hospitals, government tenders and large chains bargain strongly; individual patients have little power |
| Supplier power | High when an API comes from few sources (import dependence) |

**Competitor analysis** asks: who are the competitors, what are their strategies, objectives, strengths and weaknesses, and how will they react? Competitors can be leaders, challengers, followers or nichers.

## 1.6 Consumer buying behaviour

**Consumer buying behaviour** is how individuals and households buy goods for personal use. For medicines this mainly applies to **OTC products** and to the patient's choice of doctor and chemist.

**Factors that influence buying behaviour**

| Group | Factors |
| --- | --- |
| Cultural | Culture, subculture, social class |
| Social | Family, reference groups, roles and status |
| Personal | Age, life-cycle stage, occupation, income, lifestyle, personality |
| Psychological | Motivation, perception, learning, beliefs and attitudes |

**Buyer decision process (five stages)**

```text
Need recognition -> Information search -> Evaluation of alternatives
        -> Purchase decision -> Post-purchase behaviour
```

Example: a person with acidity (need) asks the chemist and family (search), compares an antacid gel and tablets (evaluation), buys one (decision), and buys it again if it worked (post-purchase satisfaction or dissonance).

**Maslow's hierarchy of needs** (physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualisation) explains motivation; health products serve safety needs first.

## 1.7 Industrial (organisational) buying behaviour

Organisations such as hospitals, government medical stores and companies buying raw materials buy differently from individuals.

| Feature | Industrial buying |
| --- | --- |
| Buyers | Fewer but larger |
| Decision | Group decision (buying centre), formal procedure |
| Demand | Derived from the demand for final products or services |
| Process | Specifications, tenders, quotations, negotiation, contracts |
| Relationship | Long-term, close buyer–seller relations |

**Buying centre roles:** users (doctors, nurses), influencers (pharmacy and therapeutics committee), buyers (purchase officer), deciders (medical superintendent or committee), gatekeepers (who control information).

**Buying situations:** straight rebuy, modified rebuy, new task.

**Stages:** problem recognition → general need description → product specification → supplier search → proposal (tender) → supplier selection → order routine → performance review.

## 1.8 The pharmaceutical market

### Quantitative and qualitative aspects

- **Quantitative aspects** describe how much: value and volume of sales, number of companies, number of brands, growth rate, share of each therapy area, number of doctors and chemists. These are measured by market research audits of retail sales and prescriptions. Exact figures change every year, so always quote them from a current, named source.
- **Qualitative aspects** describe what the market is like: who prescribes, why they choose a brand, attitudes of patients, influence of chemists, quality image of companies, ethical standards.

### Size and composition

The Indian market is mainly a **branded generics** market: many companies sell the same molecule under their own brand names. It can be divided by:

| Basis | Divisions |
| --- | --- |
| Prescription status | Prescription (ethical) drugs vs OTC products |
| Patent status | Patented, off-patent branded generics, unbranded (trade) generics |
| Therapy area | Anti-infectives, cardiac, gastrointestinal, anti-diabetic, pain, respiratory, vitamins and others |
| Channel | Retail (chemist) market vs institutional (hospital, government) market |
| Company origin | Indian companies vs multinational companies |
| Geography | Domestic vs export; urban vs rural |

India is also a major exporter of generic medicines, and the domestic market is highly fragmented with intense competition.

### Demographic and socio-psychological description of the consumer

- **Demographic description:** age, sex, income, education, occupation, location (urban/rural), family size, disease pattern. Example: a cardiac product targets older urban adults.
- **Socio-psychological characteristics:** attitudes to health, belief in a doctor's advice, fear of side effects, trust in brands, tendency to self-medicate, cultural beliefs about medicines, lifestyle.

## 1.9 Market segmentation and targeting

**Market segmentation** is dividing a market into distinct groups of buyers with similar needs or characteristics who may need separate products or marketing mixes.

**Bases of segmentation**

| Basis | Variables | Pharma example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Geographic | Region, state, urban/rural, climate | Rural-focused division with low-cost packs |
| Demographic | Age, sex, income | Paediatric syrups, products for women |
| Psychographic | Lifestyle, personality, values | Health-conscious buyers of supplements |
| Behavioural | Usage rate, loyalty, benefits sought | Chronic vs acute users |
| Prescriber-based | Speciality, type of practice, prescribing volume | Cardiologists, general practitioners, gynaecologists |

**Requirements of good segments:** measurable, substantial (large enough), accessible, differentiable, actionable.

**Targeting** is evaluating each segment's attractiveness and selecting one or more to enter. Strategies:

1. **Undifferentiated** — one offer for the whole market.
2. **Differentiated** — different offers for several segments (separate divisions for cardiology, gynaecology, etc.).
3. **Concentrated (niche)** — one segment served deeply (only oncology or only dermatology).
4. **Micromarketing** — local or individual targeting.

**Positioning** then fixes the product's place in the customer's mind against competitors (see Unit 2). The sequence is **segmentation → targeting → positioning (STP)**.

## 1.10 Consumer profile

A **consumer profile** is a description of the typical user of a product: age, sex, disease, severity, income, purchasing power, where they live, who influences them, and how they buy (prescription or self-selection). For ethical drugs the profile has two parts — the **prescriber profile** (speciality, patient load, prescribing habits) and the **patient profile**.

## 1.11 Motivation and prescribing habits of the physician

A doctor's choice of brand depends on:

| Factor | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Efficacy and safety | Clinical evidence, own experience with patients |
| Company image | Trust in quality and consistency of the manufacturer |
| Information sources | Medical representatives, journals, conferences (CME), colleagues, key opinion leaders |
| Patient factors | Affordability, dosing convenience, taste for children |
| Availability | Brand stocked at nearby chemists |
| Habit and loyalty | Familiar brands are repeated |
| Service | Regular, informed visits by representatives; scientific literature |

Doctors are motivated by better patient outcomes, professional reputation, up-to-date knowledge and convenience. Ethical promotion appeals to these, not to personal gifts (gifts and hospitality to doctors are restricted by the doctors' ethics regulations and the pharmaceutical marketing code).

## 1.12 Patient's choice of physician and retail pharmacist

**Choice of physician:** reputation and recommendation by family or friends, qualification and speciality, distance and availability, fees, behaviour and time given to the patient, hospital attachment.

**Choice of retail pharmacist (chemist):** nearness to home or clinic, availability of all prescribed items, price and discounts, trust and advice given, home delivery, opening hours, credit facility for regular customers. The pharmacist strongly influences OTC purchases and, where substitution happens, generic choice.

## 1.13 Analysing the market and the role of market research

**Market analysis** studies market size, growth, segments, competitors, channels and customer behaviour before decisions are made.

**Market research** is the systematic design, collection, analysis and reporting of data relevant to a specific marketing situation.

**Process**

```text
1 Define the problem and objectives
2 Develop the research plan (sources, methods, sample)
3 Collect data (secondary first, then primary)
4 Analyse and interpret
5 Report findings and recommend action
```

**Data sources**

- **Secondary data** — company sales records, published audits of retail sales and prescriptions, journals, government reports.
- **Primary data** — surveys of doctors and chemists, interviews, focus groups, observation, test marketing.

**Role in the pharmaceutical industry**

1. Estimating market size and demand for a new product.
2. Studying prescribing behaviour and brand share.
3. Testing a new brand name, pack, or promotional message.
4. Evaluating the effect of a promotional campaign and field force.
5. Studying competitors' products and prices.
6. Finding unmet needs for new product ideas.
7. Sales forecasting and territory planning.

## Remember

- Marketing starts with customer needs; selling starts with the product.
- The 4 Ps: product, price, place, promotion.
- Societal marketing concept suits medicines best.
- Micro-environment: company, suppliers, intermediaries, customers, competitors, publics; macro: demographic, economic, political–legal, technological, social–cultural, natural.
- Porter's five forces: rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power.
- Buyer decision: need → search → evaluation → purchase → post-purchase.
- Industrial buying uses a buying centre and tenders.
- STP: segmentation → targeting → positioning.
- The doctor is the key decision-maker for prescription drugs; the chemist influences OTC and generic choice.
- Never quote a market-size figure without its source and year.

# Unit 2: Product decisions

The product is the heart of the marketing mix. Price, promotion and distribution only make sense once the company knows what it is selling, to whom, and how it differs from competitors. In pharmacy the "product" is not just the molecule: it includes the dosage form, strength, pack, brand name, label, quality image, and the information and service that come with it.

## 2.1 What is a product?

A **product** is anything that can be offered to a market for attention, acquisition, use or consumption that might satisfy a want or need. It includes physical goods, services, ideas and information.

**Three levels of a product**

```text
   +-------------------------------------------+
   | AUGMENTED PRODUCT                          |
   |  patient leaflets, medical information,    |
   |  doctor support, availability, complaint   |
   |  handling, patient-support programmes      |
   |   +-----------------------------------+    |
   |   | ACTUAL PRODUCT                     |    |
   |   |  brand name, dosage form, strength,|    |
   |   |  pack, label, quality, taste       |    |
   |   |   +---------------------------+    |    |
   |   |   | CORE BENEFIT               |    |    |
   |   |   |  relief, cure, prevention  |    |    |
   |   |   +---------------------------+    |    |
   |   +-----------------------------------+    |
   +-------------------------------------------+
```

## 2.2 Classification of products

**General classification**

| Basis | Classes |
| --- | --- |
| Durability | Durable goods, non-durable goods, services |
| Consumer goods | Convenience (staple, impulse, emergency), shopping, speciality, unsought |
| Industrial goods | Materials and parts, capital items, supplies and services |

**Pharmaceutical classification**

| Basis | Classes and examples |
| --- | --- |
| Legal / sale status | Prescription (ethical) drugs, including scheduled drugs (Schedule H, H1, X); OTC (non-prescription) products |
| Patent status | Patented new drugs; off-patent branded generics; unbranded generics |
| Therapeutic class | Anti-infectives, cardiovascular, anti-diabetic, analgesics, respiratory, gastrointestinal, vitamins and supplements |
| Dosage form | Tablets, capsules, liquids, injections, topicals, inhalers |
| Nature of molecule | Small molecules, biologics and biosimilars, vaccines |
| Buyer | Retail (consumer through chemist) vs institutional (hospital, government) |
| Lifecycle of therapy | Acute-therapy products vs chronic-therapy products (repeat use) |

**Why classification matters:** a prescription drug is promoted to doctors through medical representatives, while an OTC product can be advertised to consumers; chronic-therapy products need focus on patient adherence and continuity; institutional products are sold by tender.

## 2.3 Product line and product mix decisions

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product item | A specific version (strength, form, pack) | Brand X 500 mg tablet, strip of 10 |
| Product line | A group of closely related products | All of the company's anti-diabetic brands |
| Product mix (portfolio) | All lines and items a company sells | Cardiac + diabetic + gastro + anti-infective lines |

**Dimensions of the product mix**

- **Width** — number of product lines.
- **Length** — total number of items in all lines.
- **Depth** — number of versions of each product (strengths, forms, pack sizes).
- **Consistency** — how closely the lines are related in use, production or distribution.

**Product line decisions**

1. **Line length** — too short: lost opportunities; too long: higher cost and confusion.
2. **Line stretching** — downward (cheaper versions), upward (premium versions), two-way.
3. **Line filling** — adding items within the present range (a new strength, a paediatric syrup, a sustained-release form).
4. **Line modernisation** — updating packs and forms (from tablet to orally disintegrating tablet).
5. **Line featuring** — promoting a few items to attract attention to the whole line.
6. **Line pruning** — dropping slow-moving, unprofitable or outdated products.

**Product mix strategies:** expand the mix (new lines, new therapy divisions), contract it (drop weak lines), alter existing products, or **line extension** (new combination, new dosage form of a successful brand).

## 2.4 Product life cycle (PLC)

The **product life cycle** describes the sales and profit of a product over its life in the market.

```text
 Sales / profit
   ^
   |                    _______ sales
   |                 _-'        '-_
   |              _-'              '-_
   |           _-'   ....profit....   '-_
   |        _-'   ..'            '..     '
   |   ___-'   ..'                  '..
   |__'_____..'__________________________'...__> Time
     Intro-   Growth     Maturity      Decline
     duction
```

| Stage | Sales | Profit | Competition | Marketing focus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Introduction | Low, slow growth | Negative or low (high launch cost) | Few | Create awareness among doctors; detailing, samples, CME, launch meetings |
| Growth | Rapid rise | Rising | Increasing | Build brand preference; widen distribution; new strengths |
| Maturity | Peak, slowing | Highest, then levelling | Many (branded generics) | Defend share; reminder promotion, line extensions, new indications, pack changes |
| Decline | Falling | Falling | Fewer | Reduce cost, harvest, or withdraw; shift to low-cost segments |

**Strategies to extend the life cycle:** new indication or new patient group, new dosage form or delivery system, fixed-dose combinations where rational, new pack sizes, entry into new geographic or rural markets, and switching a suitable prescription drug to OTC status where the law allows.

**Pharma features:** patent expiry causes a sharp fall in price and share of the innovator as generics enter; in branded-generic markets many brands of the same molecule are in maturity at the same time.

## 2.5 Product portfolio analysis

**Portfolio analysis** evaluates all products (or strategic business units) to decide where to invest, hold or withdraw.

### BCG growth–share matrix

```text
                 Relative market share
                 HIGH             LOW
             +--------------+--------------+
 Market  H   |   STAR       |  QUESTION    |
 growth  I   |  invest to   |  MARK        |
 rate    G   |  grow        |  invest or   |
         H   |              |  drop        |
             +--------------+--------------+
         L   |  CASH COW    |   DOG        |
         O   |  milk; funds |  harvest or  |
         W   |  others      |  divest      |
             +--------------+--------------+
```

- **Star** — high growth, high share; needs investment, becomes a cash cow later.
- **Cash cow** — low growth, high share; earns more cash than it needs (a well-established mature brand).
- **Question mark (problem child)** — high growth, low share; needs cash, may become a star or fail.
- **Dog** — low growth, low share; candidate for pruning.

### GE–McKinsey matrix

A 3 × 3 grid of **industry attractiveness** (high, medium, low) against **business strength** (strong, average, weak). Green cells = invest/grow, yellow = selective, red = harvest/divest. It uses many factors, not just growth and share.

### Ansoff product–market grid (growth strategies)

| | Existing products | New products |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Existing markets | Market penetration | Product development |
| New markets | Market development | Diversification |

## 2.6 Product positioning

**Positioning** is arranging for a product to occupy a clear, distinctive and desirable place in the target customer's mind relative to competitors.

**Bases of positioning**

| Basis | Example message |
| --- | --- |
| Attribute or feature | Once-daily dosing, sugar-free, fast dissolving |
| Benefit | Better compliance, faster relief |
| Use or application | For travellers' diarrhoea, for children |
| User | For the elderly, for pregnancy |
| Against a competitor | Fewer side effects than older agents |
| Quality / price | Premium quality, or affordable for long-term therapy |
| Product class | A modern alternative to an older class |

**Steps:** identify competitive advantages → choose the right ones (important, distinctive, superior, communicable, affordable, profitable) → communicate them consistently. A **perceptual map** plots brands on two attributes (for example price and efficacy) to find gaps.

**Unique selling proposition (USP)** — the single strongest reason a doctor should prescribe this brand. Claims must be supported by evidence and approved product information.

## 2.7 New product decisions

**Sources of new products in pharma:** in-house research, in-licensing, acquisitions, contract or co-marketing arrangements, new formulations and combinations of known molecules, and launches of generics after patent expiry.

**Types of new products:** new-to-the-world products, new product lines, additions to existing lines, improvements, repositioned products, lower-cost versions.

**New product development process**

```text
1 Idea generation       -> doctors, R&D, competitors, market research
2 Idea screening        -> drop ideas that do not fit or cannot be made
3 Concept development and testing
4 Marketing strategy    -> target, positioning, price, launch budget
5 Business analysis     -> sales, cost and profit estimates
6 Product development   -> formulation, stability, regulatory approval
7 Test marketing        -> limited areas or limited divisions
8 Commercialisation     -> launch: when, where, to whom, how
```

**Why new products fail:** wrong market estimate, poor positioning, no real advantage over existing brands, poor timing, high price, weak promotion, regulatory delay, quality problems.

**Adoption process by doctors:** awareness → interest → evaluation → trial → adoption. Adopter categories: innovators, early adopters (often key opinion leaders), early majority, late majority, laggards.

## 2.8 Branding decisions

A **brand** is a name, term, sign, symbol, design or a combination that identifies a seller's product and differentiates it from competitors. The **trademark** is the legally protected brand.

**Benefits of branding:** identifies the product, builds loyalty and repeat prescription, supports a premium, legal protection, helps new product introduction under a known family name.

**Qualities of a good pharmaceutical brand name**

- Short, easy to say, spell and remember.
- Distinctive; not confusing with other brands (look-alike and sound-alike names cause dispensing errors).
- Suggests a benefit or therapy area without making false claims.
- Legally registrable as a trademark.
- Acceptable in different languages and regions.

**Branding strategies**

| Strategy | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Individual brand names | Each product has its own brand |
| Family (umbrella) brand | One name across many products |
| Company name + individual name | Company name gives trust, brand gives identity |
| Brand extension | A known brand used for a new form or combination |
| Generic (unbranded) | Sold under the non-proprietary name |
| Co-marketing | Two companies sell the same molecule under different brands |

**Brand equity** is the added value a brand name gives a product (awareness, perceived quality, loyalty, associations).

## 2.9 Packaging decisions

**Packaging** is designing and making the container or wrapper of a product.

**Levels:** primary (in contact with the product: blister, bottle, ampoule), secondary (carton holding the primary pack), tertiary or shipping pack (corrugated box for transport).

**Functions of pharmaceutical packaging**

1. **Protection** — from light, moisture, oxygen, contamination and breakage, so the product stays stable until expiry.
2. **Identification and information** — through the label.
3. **Convenience** — unit-dose strips, calendar packs, measuring cups, droppers.
4. **Safety** — tamper-evident and child-resistant closures.
5. **Promotion** — distinctive colours and design help recognition at the chemist.
6. **Compliance** — pack size matched to course length.

**Packaging decisions:** material (glass, plastic, aluminium), form (strip, blister, bottle), pack size, design and colour, cost, compatibility and stability data, and environmental concerns.

## 2.10 Labelling decisions

The **label** carries information printed on or attached to the pack. In India labelling of drugs must follow the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.

**Information usually required on a drug label:** name of the drug (proprietary and non-proprietary name), content of active ingredients per unit, net content, batch number, manufacturing licence number, date of manufacture and date of expiry, name and address of the manufacturer, and the maximum retail price. Scheduled drugs carry the prescribed warnings (for example the Rx symbol and the Schedule H or H1 caution).

**Marketing role of labels:** identifies and grades the product, describes it, promotes through design, and protects the company legally by giving proper directions and warnings.

## 2.11 Product management in the pharmaceutical industry

In most companies a **product manager** (or brand manager) is responsible for a group of brands, like a "mini general manager" for those products.

**Duties of a product manager**

- Studying the market, competitors and prescription trends for the brands.
- Preparing the annual **brand plan**: objectives, target doctors, positioning, promotional strategy, budget, sales forecast.
- Designing promotional inputs: visual aids, literature, samples, gifts within the code, digital material.
- Training medical representatives on product knowledge and selling messages.
- Coordinating with sales, production, medical, regulatory, finance and distribution.
- Planning new product launches and line extensions.
- Monitoring sales, market share and promotional effectiveness; correcting the plan.
- Handling product complaints and feedback from the field.

**Organisation:** product managers usually report to a group product manager, who reports to the marketing head. Strength: focused attention on each brand. Weakness: responsibility without full authority over the sales force.

## Remember

- Product levels: core benefit → actual product → augmented product.
- Mix dimensions: width, length, depth, consistency.
- PLC: introduction, growth, maturity, decline; extend it with new indications, forms, packs and markets.
- BCG: star, cash cow, question mark, dog.
- Ansoff: penetration, market development, product development, diversification.
- Positioning gives a clear place in the customer's mind; claims must be backed by evidence.
- New product process: idea → screening → concept → strategy → business analysis → development → test market → launch.
- A good brand name is short, distinctive and not confusing with other drug names.
- Packaging protects, informs, assists use and promotes; labels must follow the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules.
- The product manager plans and controls the brands.

# Unit 3: Promotion

Promotion is the communication part of marketing: telling the right people about a product, persuading them that it meets their need, and reminding them to keep using it. In pharmacy, promotion is shaped by a special fact: for prescription medicines the target is the doctor (and pharmacist), not the patient, and the message must be scientific, balanced and within the law.

## 3.1 Meaning and objectives of promotion

**Promotion** is the coordination of all seller-initiated efforts to set up channels of information and persuasion in order to sell goods or services or promote an idea.

**Objectives of pharmaceutical promotion**

1. **Inform** — create awareness of a new product, its indications, dose forms and evidence.
2. **Persuade** — build preference for the brand over competitors.
3. **Remind** — keep the brand in the doctor's mind (reminder detailing, reminder items).
4. **Educate** — continuing medical education (CME) on diseases and rational use.
5. **Build image** — present the company as reliable and quality-focused.
6. **Support the trade** — help chemists and stockists stock and sell the product.

**AIDA model** of how promotion works: **Attention → Interest → Desire → Action** (prescription or purchase).

## 3.2 Methods (tools) of promotion — the promotional mix

| Tool | Description | Main use in pharma |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal selling | Face-to-face presentation by a sales representative | Detailing prescription drugs to doctors — the main tool |
| Advertising | Paid, non-personal communication by an identified sponsor | Journal advertisements to professionals; mass media only for OTC products |
| Sales promotion | Short-term incentives to encourage trial or purchase | Physician samples, trade schemes for chemists, consumer offers on OTC packs |
| Public relations | Building good relations with publics and a favourable image | Health camps, disease awareness, press releases, sponsorship of CME |
| Direct marketing | Direct communication with targeted individuals | Direct mail, e-mail, messages to doctors |
| Digital / online | Websites, social media, search, apps, e-detailing | OTC consumer reach; scientific content for professionals |

**Push versus pull strategy**

- **Push** — promotion is directed at channel members and prescribers, who "push" the product to the next level (detailing, trade schemes).
- **Pull** — promotion is directed at final consumers, who "pull" the product through the channel by asking for it (mainly OTC advertising).
- Prescription drugs rely mostly on push through doctors; OTC products use more pull.

## 3.3 Determinants of the promotional mix

The right mix depends on:

| Determinant | Effect on the mix |
| --- | --- |
| Type of product | Prescription drugs: personal selling, journals, samples; OTC: advertising, retail display |
| Type of market / target | Few, technical buyers (doctors, hospitals) → personal selling; mass consumers → advertising |
| Stage of product life cycle | Introduction: heavy detailing, samples, launch meets; growth: build preference; maturity: reminders, trade schemes; decline: minimum spend |
| Buyer readiness stage | Awareness and knowledge → advertising, PR; conviction and purchase → personal selling |
| Push or pull strategy | Push → field force and trade; pull → consumer advertising |
| Available budget | Small budgets favour focused personal selling and direct mail |
| Competition | Match or out-do competitors' share of voice |
| Legal and ethical rules | Restrict who and how a product may be promoted |

## 3.4 Promotional budget

The **promotional budget** is the money set aside for all promotional activities for a period.

**Methods of setting the budget**

1. **Affordable method** — spend what the company thinks it can afford; simple but ignores market needs.
2. **Percentage-of-sales method** — a fixed percentage of current or expected sales; easy, but treats sales as the cause of promotion rather than its result.
3. **Competitive-parity method** — match competitors' spending; avoids promotion wars but assumes competitors are right.
4. **Objective-and-task method** — define objectives, list the tasks needed (number of calls, samples, meetings, advertisements), cost them, and add up; the most logical method.

**Main items in a pharma promotional budget:** field force costs, samples, literature and visual aids, journal advertising, conferences and CME support, digital promotion, reminder items, market research.

## 3.5 Personal selling (overview)

Personal selling is the most important promotional tool for prescription drugs. The **medical representative** (professional sales representative, PSR) visits doctors, explains the product with scientific evidence (**detailing**), answers questions, gives samples and literature, and also visits chemists and stockists. Its strengths are two-way communication, flexibility and relationship building; its weakness is high cost per contact. Details of the PSR are in Unit 4.

**Steps in personal selling:** prospecting and pre-call planning → approach → presentation (detailing) → handling objections → closing (asking for prescriptions) → follow-up.

## 3.6 Advertising

**Advertising** is any paid form of non-personal presentation of ideas, goods or services by an identified sponsor.

**Types**

- **Product advertising** — informative (new product), persuasive (build preference), reminder (mature product).
- **Institutional (corporate) advertising** — builds the company's image.

**Media:** medical journals, newspapers and magazines, television and radio (OTC only), outdoor, internet and social media, point-of-sale material at chemists.

**Legal limits in India (overview)**

- The **Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954** prohibits advertisements claiming to cure the diseases and conditions listed in its schedule, and misleading claims about drugs.
- Under the **Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945**, drugs may not be advertised to the public as preventing or curing the diseases and ailments listed in Schedule J.
- Prescription medicines are promoted to registered medical practitioners and pharmacists, not advertised to the general public.
- The **Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP)** issued by the Department of Pharmaceuticals (first in 2014, revised in 2024) requires claims to be accurate, balanced, up to date and supported by evidence, and restricts gifts, travel and hospitality to healthcare professionals.

**Developing an advertising programme (5 Ms):** Mission (objectives), Money (budget), Message (what to say), Media (where), Measurement (evaluation of recall and sales effect).

## 3.7 Direct mail

**Direct mail** is promotional material posted (or sent electronically) directly to selected doctors, pharmacists or consumers.

- **Content:** product leaflets, reprints of published studies, newsletters, reminder cards, invitations to CME.
- **Advantages:** reaches doctors the field force cannot visit often (remote areas, busy specialists), selective, personal, low cost per contact, easy to test.
- **Limitations:** often discarded unread, needs a correct and updated mailing list, no two-way discussion.
- Today much direct mail is replaced by e-mail newsletters and messaging, which must respect consent and privacy.

## 3.8 Journals (journal advertising)

Medical and pharmacy journals carry advertisements and sponsored inserts aimed at professionals.

- **Advantages:** reaches a targeted professional audience; credibility of the journal; the advertisement stays in the issue for repeated viewing; supports detailing.
- **Limitations:** cluttered with many advertisements; cannot be personalised; effect is hard to measure.
- **Good practice:** include the generic name, approved indications, and a reference to full prescribing information; claims must be supported by evidence.

## 3.9 Sampling

**Physician samples** are small quantities of a product given free to doctors so that they can become familiar with it and try it in their patients.

**Purposes:** encourage trial of a new product, remind about an existing brand, help start therapy, support patients who cannot afford a full course (at the doctor's discretion).

**Good sampling practice**

- Give samples only to doctors qualified to prescribe the product.
- Mark samples "Physician's sample — not to be sold".
- Give a reasonable quantity; keep records of samples given.
- Store samples properly; follow the marketing code's limits.
- Never sell samples or give them as an inducement.

**Limitations:** costly, can be misused or sold, and may encourage unneeded prescribing if overused.

## 3.10 Retailing (retail promotion)

The retail chemist is the final link to the patient. **Retail promotion** aims to make sure the product is stocked, visible and recommended.

**Methods:** window and counter displays, shelf space, posters, dispensers, point-of-purchase material for OTC products, trade schemes (bonus quantities, discounts within regulated margins), chemist meetings, product information for pharmacists, and prompt supply and credit.

**Role of the pharmacist:** gives advice on OTC products, ensures correct dispensing, may suggest a brand where substitution is permitted, and is a source of market feedback.

## 3.11 Medical exhibitions

Companies set up **stalls at medical conferences, CMEs and exhibitions** to meet many doctors in one place.

**Advantages:** contact with many specialists at low cost per contact; launch of new products; demonstration of devices; collection of doctors' feedback and names; builds company image.

**Planning an exhibition stall:** choose the right conference (speciality matches the products), design an attractive and informative stall, send trained representatives and medical advisers, prepare literature and visual material, keep a register of visitors, and follow up after the event.

## 3.12 Public relations

**Public relations (PR)** builds goodwill and a favourable image with the company's various publics: doctors, patients, government, media, employees, investors and the local community.

**Tools:** press releases and media relations, health camps and screening camps, disease-awareness campaigns, sponsorship of scientific events within the code, corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities, publications and newsletters, crisis management (product recall communication).

**Value:** high credibility (news is believed more than advertisements), low cost, protects reputation in a crisis, supports all other promotion.

## 3.13 Online promotional techniques for OTC products

OTC (non-prescription) products can be promoted to consumers, and online methods are now central.

| Technique | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Company and brand websites | Product information, usage directions, FAQs |
| Search engine optimisation and search advertising | Appear when consumers search a symptom or product |
| Social media marketing | Brand pages, short videos, health tips, responding to queries |
| Influencer marketing | Endorsement by health or lifestyle creators (with disclosure) |
| E-mail and messaging marketing | Newsletters and offers to subscribed users |
| Display and video advertising | Banners and video ads on websites and apps |
| E-commerce and online pharmacy listings | Product pages, ratings, offers on online platforms |
| Mobile apps | Reminders, health trackers linked to brands |
| Content marketing | Articles and videos on health topics that build trust |

**Precautions:** claims must be truthful and permitted for that product; no promotion of prescription drugs to consumers; no claims for Schedule J diseases or those under the Objectionable Advertisements Act; respect privacy and data-protection rules; monitor online comments for adverse event reports.

**Advantages:** wide reach, precise targeting, low cost, measurable results (clicks, views, conversions), two-way interaction.

## 3.14 Ethics in pharmaceutical promotion

- Information must be accurate, balanced, fair, objective and supported by evidence.
- Do not hide side effects or contraindications.
- No misleading comparisons with competitors.
- No inducements (cash, costly gifts, travel) to doctors to prescribe.
- Samples only for evaluation, never for sale.
- The WHO's *Ethical Criteria for Medicinal Drug Promotion* (1988) also guide these standards.

## Remember

- Promotion informs, persuades and reminds; AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action.
- Promotional mix: personal selling, advertising, sales promotion, PR, direct marketing, digital.
- Prescription drugs → push through doctors; OTC → pull through consumers.
- Budget methods: affordable, percentage of sales, competitive parity, objective-and-task (best).
- Samples are marked "not to be sold" and given only to prescribers.
- Exhibitions reach many doctors at once; PR builds credibility.
- OTC online tools: websites, search, social media, e-mail, apps, e-commerce listings.
- Law and code: Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954, Schedule J of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, UCPMP.
